items.title: ‘Craving the Truth’: The Shocking Spiritual Hunger Sweeping Gen Z
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Naomi Anderson is on a mission to point Generation Z toward the truth.

Anderson is co-founder of Verity Collective, “a movement rooted in the unchanging truth of the Gospel.” She told CBN News she wants to bring Jesus to America’s young generation.

Listen to the latest episode of “Quick Start”

“We believe that there is a lot of confusion and noise in this world for them, and we want to bring them back to the one and only truth, which is Jesus,” she said.

Anderson believes young people are “craving the truth” but have faced an uphill battle in understanding it, as they’ve been sold an improper understanding of reality.

“They are craving the truth. They just don’t know what it is because they’ve been told to define it for themselves,” she said. “So when we ask them, ‘What is truth?’ they literally will sit there on camera and it will take them minutes to try to decide right because they have been told truth is objective — you can define your own truth. … They just need to be pointed back to the truth.”

The need for truth couldn’t be more pressing, as many young people are suffering from mental health issues, including anxiety and depression.

“It all forms around this idea of what is my identity, and where am I grounded in, and they just don’t have a landing solid spot,” Anderson said.

She also noted that young men appear to be increasingly interested in the Christian faith.

“These men are craving solid biblical truth, and that only comes from reading your Bible, and picking up the word, and being taught it by a Bible teacher,” Anderson said.

Through Verity Collective, she’s hoping to visit college campuses across the US in September and have a presence to spark conversations.

“What we’re recognizing is that when you actually pull someone aside and start asking them questions like, ‘What is truth?’ they have a yearning to know what it is that you want them to know,” Anderson said. “They’ll ask … ‘What do you believe truth is?’ And it really does open up an opportunity for us to speak the Gospel of Jesus Christ to them. And they are excited to hear it.”

Find out more about Verity Collective here.

items.title: Christian Activist Sues Minnesota City for Putting ‘Price Tag’ on His Constitutional Rights
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: A Christian man from Minnesota was ordered to pay for his free speech rights — and now he's suing.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

A Christian man from Minnesota was ordered to pay for his free speech rights — and now he’s suing.

In a lawsuit filed by the Center for American Liberty, Bryan Conwell is accusing officials in Benson of severe First Amendment violations by placing a “price tag” on free speech after Cherie Stielow, now a city council member, forced him to purchase a commercial vendor’s license to practice his constitutionally protected right to free speech at the city’s farmers market, which Stielow facilitates.

“Government officials cannot force Americans to buy a license before they peacefully express their beliefs on public property,” Mark Trammell of the Center for American Liberty said in a statement about the case. “If they can silence Bryan today, they can silence anyone tomorrow.”

According to the legal complaint, Conwell regularly holds pro-life and Gospel-centered placards on public property and waits peacefully and silently, speaking only to those who initiate conversation with him. The suit states the Christian activist “blocks no one, threatens no one, and sells nothing,” adding, “He asks only to be left alone to speak.”

Conwell, according to court documents, initially paid the $20 fee in order to hold his signs on public property during the hours the market was operating. In 2023, when he filled out the form and complied with the financial request, Conwell “was unaware of what his rights were and was simply trying to ensure that he could convey his message,” the complaint states.

The city then allowed Conwell to be present at the market in September and October 2023, but only so long as he remained inside a vendor tent.

At the same time as the dustup with Stielow was underway, another thread of Conwell’s story was unraveling.

In late July 2023, when all this began, the street preacher stood in a grassy area near the farmers market and spoke using a sound amplifier. At about 30 minutes to an hour into his speaking, Police Chief Ian Hodge purportedly told him he was breaking the city’s 50-foot sound ordinance and needed a permit to continue, so Conwell stopped.

Then between Aug. 9 and Oct. 24 of that year, Conwell made four separate trips to city hall, where he repeatedly attempted to apply for and obtain said noise permit. According to court documents, he was seemingly given the runaround by the city clerk, who said she was not aware of any such permit. He was also told the relevant person was unavailable and on more than one occasion was asked for his contact information but received no follow-up communication.

That saga came to an abrupt end on Oct. 24, 2023, when Hodge and the city attorney informed Conwell no such permit existed.

When Conwell returned to Benson on July 9 of this year and was approached yet again by Stielow, who handed him a vendor permit and demanded $20, he declined outright, reminding her — as in 2023 — he was not selling anything and would not be paying to hold a sign and speak peacefully with people on public property. He attempted the same thing on July 16.

Conwell received a trespass citation in both 2026 instances. He now faces up to 90 days in jail and up to $2,000 in fines.

Even one of the officers who cited Conwell purportedly expressed confusion to the preacher over the city’s policy against speech that should be protected by the Constitution.

“To be honest, man, I want clarification, too,” the officer told Conwell, according to court filings. “There are crimes of trespassing and crimes of disorderly conduct, but also you have your First Amendment right, so we’ve got to try to figure that out. … I know what you’re doing, I get it. I’m glad someone is out here doing it.”

items.title: New Life for Dead Hearts
items.author: Elisa Morgan
items.summary: Heartwood is the central supporting pillar of certain trees. Although dead, it won’t decay or lose strength while the outer, living layers are intact. Composed of fibers bound together by a chemical glue called lignin, heartwood can be as strong as steel. This element of a tree’s structu
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

Heartwood is the central supporting pillar of certain trees. Although dead, it won’t decay or lose strength while the outer, living layers are intact. Composed of fibers bound together by a chemical glue called lignin, heartwood can be as strong as steel. This element of a tree’s structure enables it to survive nature’s travails.

When Paul encouraged the Colossians to live a resurrected life, he could have used the metaphor of heartwood to express how those who have been saved, are transformed. “For you died, and your life is now hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:3). While Paul’s reference to us as “dead” might seem discouraging, when understood from the perspective of the resurrection we grasp the hope of such a statement. God transforms the dead core of our beings, strengthening us in the power of the resurrected Jesus to endure the trials of this life.

Our prior inner beings are as dead as the heartwood of a tree. Yet we still exist as the unique people God created us to be—and more. We’re made new (Revelation 21:5). We’re new creatures in Christ (2 Corinthians 5:17). In Jesus “we live and move and have our being” (Acts 17:28).

We see a living example of how the structure of trees represents our life in Christ. Thanks be to God for transforming us from death to life!

items.title: The Company We Keep
items.author: Marvin Williams
items.summary: A scientific study revealed that watching TV programs featuring mean characters can actually lead people to be mean. Various forms of aggression—whether outright fighting or subtle gossip—primes viewers’ brains for similar behavior. This connection is often subconscious, meaning th
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

A scientific study revealed that watching TV programs featuring mean characters can actually lead people to be mean. Various forms of aggression—whether outright fighting or subtle gossip—primes viewers’ brains for similar behavior. This connection is often subconscious, meaning that even shows with seemingly “harmless” jokes at others’ expense can subtly influence how we treat others. So too, the people we choose to spend our time with will affect our behavior.

Solomon provides timeless wisdom on this important subject: “Walk with the wise and become wise, for a companion of fools suffers harm” (Proverbs 13:20). He implies that individuals may not achieve this wisdom alone, so they should associate with wise, God-honoring people—teachers and friends—instead of those who are foolish. Surrounding oneself with wise individuals fosters “good judgment” and helps us steer clear of “destruction” (v. 15). One scholar calls this “education by friendship.” Regular companions inevitably influence each other, for better or worse. Solomon urges us to be aware of the company we keep, recognizing that “the teaching of the wise is a fountain of life” (v. 14).  

As God helps us, let’s consistently surround ourselves with people who will encourage us to revere Him, love others, and grow in wisdom.

items.title: The New ‘Spider-Man’ Movie Is Getting Praise for Tackling Loneliness Head-On
items.author: Emily Brown
items.summary: After years of multiverse crossovers, nostalgia plays and increasingly universe-sized stakes, Spider-Man: Brand New Day is doing something surprisingly simple: making Peter Parker feel like Peter Parker again. The first reactions to Tom Holland’s fourth solo outing have been overwhelmingly pos
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

After years of multiverse crossovers, nostalgia plays and increasingly universe-sized stakes, Spider-Man: Brand New Day is doing something surprisingly simple: making Peter Parker feel like Peter Parker again.

The first reactions to Tom Holland’s fourth solo outing have been overwhelmingly positive, with critics calling it his best performance yet and praising director Destin Daniel Cretton for trading spectacle for something more grounded, emotional and personal. Several reviewers have called it the strongest Spider-Man film of Holland’s run, with one describing it as “a grounded Spider-Man tale” that finally leaves behind the “multiverse tedium” for a story driven by character instead of cameos.

But the praise isn’t really about the action sequences or the return to New York City. It’s about loneliness.

Following the events of No Way Home, Peter is completely alone — MJ and Ned no longer remember him, and he’s left to navigate adulthood without the people who once defined his life. Early reactions say the film leans into that isolation rather than rushing past it, with multiple critics pointing to loneliness, friendship and the slow work of rebuilding human connection as its emotional core.

That’s not incidental. Young adults report feeling more isolated than at any point in modern history, even as they stay more digitally connected than any generation before them. A Spider-Man story about grief and learning how to reconnect doesn’t arrive in a vacuum — and audiences will probably feel that.

It’s also just a reminder of why Peter Parker has always worked. He’s not compelling because he can swing between skyscrapers. He’s compelling because underneath the mask he’s a young adult trying to figure out how to carry responsibility without losing himself. Brand New Day, if the early word holds, seems to actually remember that.

The film opens July 31.

items.title: Can America Disagree Better?
items.author: Jack Trent
items.summary:
Jack Trent

A greater commitment to logic and media literacy will help more Americans see past the razzle-dazzle strategy of entertainment politics and return to sound thinking.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Jack Trent

Spencer Cox, governor of Utah, and Wes Moore, governor of Maryland, feature in a viral video in which the two men acknowledge their dissimilarities:

Cox: He’s black
Moore: And he’s white
Cox: He grew up in the city 
Moore: And he’s a farm boy from Kentucky
Cox: He’s a Democrat
Moore: And he’s a Republican

The governors then remark that despite their differences, they have meaningful similarities, they are friends, and they respect each other. Cox states that “politics is important, but it shouldn’t define us or destroy our relationships.” 

The video comes from Disagree Better, an initiative of the National Governors Association started by Cox in 2023. The Disagree Better website states, “Disagree Better isn’t about being lukewarm, acting nice, or giving up your beliefs. It’s about standing strong, having passion, and still seeing the humanity in those who disagree.” Through various initiatives, Disagree Better seeks to model healthy civic disagreement. Over twenty governors have joined the movement. 

So far so good. Disagree Better is what America needs today, especially in light of recent political violence. Still, Disagree Better is susceptible to passing away as a fad if the movement fails to clearly identify the reasons why America currently disagrees poorly. One of the reasons we Americans disagree poorly is that our political discourse takes place within a framework of entertainment and emotivism. A real commitment to disagreeing better therefore entails turning down the entertainment dial on our political discourse and returning to a recognition of objective reality. 

American Politics in the Age of Show Business 

At its founding, America was a thriving intellectual society. Thomas Paine’s Common Sense—by no means an easy read—sold 500,000 copies by the close of the American Revolution (equivalent to sixty million today). The federalist-antifederalist debates spilled beyond closed doors into pamphlets and newspapers. Large crowds attended multi-hour debates between Abraham Lincoln and Stephen Douglas. In these early days, Americans disagreed well, at least insofar as they engaged in substantive intellectual discourse. 

Today disagreeing well has become more difficult, for America has a much less serious intellectual culture than before. Neil Postman, writing in 1985, argued that America had entered an age of show business, where sights and sounds carried greater political weight than words and deeds. For Postman, the decadence of political discourse was brought about in part by the introduction of new media—most prominently, the television.

Unlike the written word, the television appeals to the senses. For Postman, entertainment is baked into the nature of television, or at least into its common practice. Television programs have short shot lengths, attractive show hosts, plenty of on-screen graphics, a pleasant backdrop, and music—“All television news programs begin, end, and are somewhere in between punctuated with music. . . . What has music to do with the news? Why is it there?” The answer, of course, is show business. 

There is nothing wrong with entertainment in its rightful place, but Postman insists that a medium ordered to entertainment cannot accommodate serious intellectual content. Attempting to translate the language of politics (which demands sobriety) into the language of entertainment (which demands charm) is a recipe for disaster. 

Said another way, the virtues of the statesmen are not the virtues of the showman. Politicians must be intelligent, prudent, measured, and collected. These are not values the television is apt to display. Postman notes, “When a television show is in process it is very nearly impermissible to say, ‘Let me think about that’ or ‘I don’t know’ or ‘What do you mean when you say . . . ?’” Such remarks, acceptable in themselves, make for a boring television program. And a boring television program is a dead television program. 

Some thirty years after Postman’s critique, our political discourse has further declined. I take the 2024 Republican Primary Debates as just one example. This televised debate opened with a 3D graphic montage played over music fit for a primetime college football game; before the candidates spoke, a ten-second clip of President Biden, a twenty-second man-on-the-street interview compilation, and a short video of a man singing with a guitar were all played; the candidates were told they would have one minute to answer each question.

Without addressing the content of the debate, I note that the debate set-up alone sends a message to the American people. It tells our country that politics is a spectacle to be watched. It is a showdown to enjoy. It is tonight’s entertainment. Moreover an entertainment-minded set-up provides no incentive for the candidates to proceed in a sober manner. It does, on the other hand, provide incentive to be witty, crass, outlandish, or otherwise memorable. America will not learn to disagree better while public debate is held in such an uncharitable and unserious way. (It is rather curious that the entertainment-ization of politics in America does not lead to its trivialization. Politics, however amusing, still retains its hold over the American mind.) 
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

With all of this said, the television—and the iPhone, for that matter—are not going anywhere. America’s political life will continue to be played out on the screen for the foreseeable future. What is to be done? How can we disagree better in our public square? 

Solutions, Logic, and Media Literacy

I have so far offered only a partial diagnosis of America’s inability to disagree better, and in like manner, I now turn to offer only a partial solution. I argue part of the task of the responsible citizen in the face of modern entertainment politics is to become logical and media literate. 

To become logical is quite the task, as most have unfortunately not received any formal training in logic (“logic” taken in a broad sense, including rhetoric, dialectic, and “critical thinking”). This is a serious omission in American education. Logic enables one to recognize and construct sound arguments. If we do not know what a good argument looks like in the first place, it is unlikely we will stumble upon appreciating or making one ourselves.

Logic also teaches us to recognize fallacious argumentation. Red herrings, non sequiturs, sunk cost fallacies, gambler’s fallacies, ad hominem attacks, and other fallacies are much easier to identify once we know what they are. Learning the vocabulary and distinctions of logic enables us to clearly and distinctly identify where we disagree with our opponents. And such intellectual precision is bound to help us disagree better. 

From the thirty-thousand-foot view, then, we should work to implement logic courses in primary, secondary, and post-secondary education. There is no telling how much good could come from future generations possessing the ability to construct sound argumentation and call out fallacious reasoning when they see it. From a more personal view, those who do not have logical training would do well to take an online course or read books on logic and critical thinking. This can be a dry, boring endeavor, but possessing a logical mind pays dividends in the long run. 

Developing media literacy will also help us disagree better. Media literacy has been described as “the ability to encode and decode the symbols transmitted via media and synthesize, analyze and produce mediated messages.” What this means in practice is the ability to discern the value of any given online post, video, or photo. A ten-second video clip of a politician delivering a spicy one-liner in a debate should not exert the same pull over our thoughts, feelings, and actions as a peer-reviewed research paper, though the former may be far more seductive.  

Media literacy entails self-awareness. Do I really think such-and-such political influencer is worth listening to? Or do I just find him to be entertaining? Do I equate entertainment with truth? Questions like these will reveal our true disposition to politics, and I suspect many of us will need to purify our intentions. 

To this end, greater media literacy will mean a greater appreciation of the “new media.” Specifically, the long-form podcast may turn out to be a rather conducive avenue for public discourse about the common good. 

The Joe Rogan Experience, though certainly imperfect, could serve as a more helpful investigation of a candidate than much of what is put on cable news. Rogan’s interviews with Bernie Sanders, JD Vance, and his three-hour interview with Donald Trump all eschewed extensive hype music, fancy graphics, flashy lighting, and scheduled commercial breaks. Such a set-up emphasizes the person and his or her ideas. This is more of what America needs. Indeed Americans may learn to disagree better simply by listening to a couple hours of a podcast featuring a guest with opposing views. 

The process of learning to disagree better is daunting, but we should avoid pessimism. A greater commitment to logic and media literacy will help more Americans see past the razzle-dazzle strategy of entertainment politics and return to sound thinking. By pursuing these ends we will learn to disagree better and treat each other as rational, dignified human persons.

items.title: Thursday, July 30, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, today’s Gospel reminds us of the final judgment, when the wicked will be separated from the righteous.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
Jeremiah 18:1-6

The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord: “Come, go down to the potter’s house, and there I will let you hear my words.” So I went down to the potter’s house, and there he was working at his wheel. The vessel he was making of clay was spoiled in the potter’s hand, and he reworked it into another vessel, as seemed good to him.

Then the word of the Lord came to me: Can I not do with you, O house of Israel, just as this potter has done? says the Lord. Just like the clay in the potter’s hand, so are you in my hand, O house of Israel.

Psalm
Psalm 146:1B-2, 3-4, 5-6ab

Praise the Lord!
Praise the Lord, O my soul!
I will praise the Lord as long as I live;
    I will sing praises to my God all my life long.
Do not put your trust in princes,
    in mortals, in whom there is no help.
When their breath departs, they return to the earth;
    on that very day their plans perish.
Happy are those whose help is the God of Jacob,
    whose hope is in the Lord their God,
who made heaven and earth,
    the sea, and all that is in them;
who keeps faith forever;

Gospel Reading
Matthew 13:47-53

Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net that was thrown into the sea and caught fish of every kind; when it was full, they drew it ashore, sat down, and put the good into baskets but threw out the bad. So it will be at the end of the age. The angels will come out and separate the evil from the righteous and throw them into the furnace of fire, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

“Have you understood all this?” They answered, “Yes.” And he said to them, “Therefore every scribe who has been trained for the kingdom of heaven is like the master of a household who brings out of his treasure what is new and what is old.” When Jesus had finished these parables, he left that place.

Reflection

Friends, today’s Gospel reminds us of the final judgment, when the wicked will be separated from the righteous. When good and evil are confused or intermingled, divine judgment separates them, clarifying the issue. 

Bob Dylan said, “The enemy I see wears the cloak of decency.” One of the favorite ruses of evil is to cover itself in the mantle of justice and piety, at the same time aping and hiding behind that which it opposes. Christ’s judgment rips away these cloaking devices, these deceits, and shows things as they are. 

Authentic Christianity is a fighting religion, and it calls evil by its name. The Church knows what stands outside of itself, and it turns its back on it. The bearer of light and truth, it separates good from evil, sometimes painfully, like a “two-edged sword.”
